recent_posts.topic_title: [DIS] FiberNuts: Reliable Cashu-over-Fiber Payments with Hosted-LSP Onboarding
recent_posts.author: Code3ks
recent_posts.content_text:
Summary
This proposal requests $6,000 USD equivalent in CKB for a 12-week development and validation phase for FiberNuts, an open Cashu-over-Fiber settlement adapter with RUSD reference applications.
FiberNuts lets a stock Cashu mint issue and redeem RUSD-denominated ecash through Fiber Network.
Users can add ecash by paying a Fiber invoice, transfer Cashu tokens directly, settle received tokens by swapping them for fresh proofs, and cash out through an external Fiber invoice. The mint remains custodial and controls issuance, swaps, and redemption.
The protocol already works. The public repository contains the Rust cdk-fiber adapter, an out-of-process processor for an unmodified cdk-mintd, a browser wallet, deployment tooling, and a Community Market application for attendee-to-vendor payments. Public testnet services are live and community members have completed the two-role payment flow.
This grant funds the next three outcomes:
settlement and refund operations that recover safely after timeouts, lost responses, and process restarts;
public-testnet hosted-LSP onboarding so users can fund and use a Fiber channel without running their own FNN node; and
a packaged cdk-fiber release, upstream contribution, independent testnet validation, Community Market pilot, and tightly capped direct-channel mainnet validation.
The grant does not fund past work, mint reserves, user deposits, or routing liquidity. It does not promise a public mainnet mint, trustless custody, guaranteed redemption, or an upstream merge.
Grant amount requested: $6,000 USD equivalent, paid in CKB at the USD value at each disbursement
ETA to completion: 12 weeks from initial disbursement
CKB receiving address: ckb1qyqvznaanauthpv49aajstw6frwc9gvg5nasjdwwnv
What FiberNuts is
FiberNuts connects Cashu bearer ecash to Fiber’s CKB and UDT payment channels:
wallet or application
|
| Cashu HTTP APIs
v
stock cdk-mintd
|
| standard payment-processor gRPC
v
fibernuts-processor + cdk-fiber
|
| Fiber JSON-RPC
v
Fiber node -> CKB
The reusable component is cdk-fiber, a Rust implementation of CDK’s MintPayment interface. It allows an unmodified cdk-mintd to advertise the fiber payment method and rusd unit without a private CDK or Fiber fork.
One operator runs one mint, processor, and Fiber settlement stack. Each mint has its own keys, database, reserves, policies, liquidity, fees, and trust boundary. FiberNuts supports independent operator mints; the project-operated reference mint is not a protocol trust anchor.
Money flow
Add cash: The wallet pays a RUSD Fiber invoice and receives Cashu proofs only after Fiber reports the invoice Paid.
Bearer payment: A sender transfers Cashu proofs directly. The recipient is settled only after the issuing mint accepts those proofs and returns fresh proofs.
Cash out: The mint spends submitted proofs and pays an external RUSD Fiber invoice. A timeout remains pending or recoverable unless Fiber reports an authoritative terminal result.
Why this work is needed
Settlement must survive interruption
The current adapter handles Fiber states conservatively, but complete operation context must survive restart and lost-response boundaries. A delayed cash-out may settle after the original call returns Pending; the processor must recover the original principal, fee, quote, and event state without sending a second payment or mutating a balance twice.
Incoming watches, outgoing correlation, RPC deadlines, event delivery, retries, reconciliation, and refund races need durable state and reproducible failure tests.
Users should not need to operate an FNN node
The current direct-channel flow assumes access to a Fiber node and usable channel liquidity. Fiber’s hosted-LSP work provides a path where an operator hosts Fiber connectivity while the client retains the required signing role.
The user still supplies on-chain RUSD and the CKB capacity required for channel creation. Hosted LSP removes local node operation and manual channel management; it is not a free on-ramp and does not remove mint custody or liquidity risk.
The required grant environment is a reproducible, project-operated public-testnet LSP. The Fiber team’s public testnet LSP will be used for interoperability testing when available, but an external service launch is not a payment condition.
Availability, liquidity, and solvency are different
A reachable mint is not necessarily solvent. Channel capacity does not prove usable directional liquidity, and successful onboarding does not guarantee later redemption. The application must show the active mint, LSP, network, exact RUSD asset, operation state, and known fees without labeling an operator as trusted, verified, liquid, or solvent without supporting evidence.
Loop is a separate liquidity layer
Fiber’s Loop work addresses rebalancing after a channel exists. FiberNuts will document the compatibility boundary but will not implement or fork Loop, operate a Loop provider, or make the draft Loop work a milestone dependency.
Work already completed
The following baseline is not funded retroactively:
cdk-fiber, implementing CDK’s payment-backend interface over Fiber JSON-RPC.
fibernuts-processor, exposing the adapter through CDK’s standard gRPC processor protocol.
Compatibility with a stock, unmodified cdk-mintd.
Conservative handling of Paid, Received, Pending, Failed, and Unknown Fiber states.
Exact network and UDT validation before a Cashu cash-out can probe or pay a Fiber route.
A browser wallet with per-mint storage, add cash, send, receive-side swap, NUT-18 requests, cash out, activity, and recoverable operation states.
A Community Market attendee application, vendor terminal, capability-scoped payment relay, and bounded public-testnet claim service.
Vendor-key-locked NUT-18 payments that the relay cannot redeem.
Docker deployment, deterministic Rust and TypeScript tests, browser tests, and opt-in live Fiber tests.
Reproducible devnet and public-testnet runbooks.
A demonstrated mint-to-transfer-to-cash-out cycle over a live three-node Fiber route with a real routing fee.
Public testnet wallet, mint, relay, claim service, and Community Market deployments.
The current implementation is pinned to Fiber v0.9.0-rc7 and CDK v0.17.2. The funded work will validate Fiber v0.9.1 and CDK v0.18.2, or newer stable versions pinned at project start, through code and tests rather than assumptions.
FiberNuts received first place and a final score of 28/30 in the relevant Fiber infrastructure category. That result is evidence of the baseline, not a request for retroactive payment.
Why now
FiberNuts has moved beyond an architecture demo: the protocol, public testnet services, bounded claim flow, and attendee-to-vendor application are available for community testing.
Public feedback now identifies concrete next barriers rather than hypothetical features: easier onboarding, restart-safe settlement, refunds, clearer risk disclosure, and reproducible operator deployment.
Fiber v0.9.1 and CDK v0.18.2 provide stable compatibility targets, while Fiber’s hosted-LSP work is active enough to define and test an operator-run public-testnet integration boundary.
Trust and responsibility boundaries
Mint operator: Holds backing RUSD, maintains the spent-proof database, controls issuance and redemption, and may charge a declared Cashu input fee or require authentication.
LSP operator: Hosts Fiber connectivity and channel runtime, may charge a declared service fee, and can affect availability and routing. The intended client-signer design does not send the user’s root signing secret to the LSP.
User: Supplies RUSD and CKB capacity, approves funding, protects client recovery material, and chooses which mint liability to hold.
Blind signatures reduce direct issuance-to-redemption linkage. They do not hide timing, amounts, network metadata, browser metadata, or operator policy. Browser proofs remain bearer secrets and are not a guaranteed backup.

documentation

Demonstrated live multi-hop RUSD settlement with conservative payment-state handling.
Received first place and a final score of 28/30 in the prior independent review.

The project runs for 12 weeks. Funding follows four equal tranches. Every tranche after initial funding follows a public milestone report and reviewer acceptance.

Milestone 1: settlement reliability and refund recovery
ETA: Weeks 1-4
Tranche: $1,500 USD equivalent
Deliverables:
Durable incoming and outgoing settlement journal keyed by CDK quote ID and Fiber payment hash.
Correct delayed-success accounting for original principal and actual routing fee.
Incoming watches and outgoing terminal events restored after processor restart.

Publish the tagged milestone release, test logs, known limitations, and recovery report.
Milestone 2: hosted-LSP public-testnet onboarding
ETA: Weeks 5-8
Tranche: $1,500 USD equivalent
Deliverables:
Typed hosted-LSP adapter isolated from wallet presentation code.
Reproducible project-operated public-testnet LSP deployment.
Tenant registration, authenticated communication, client signing, and persisted lifecycle state.
One documented CKB wallet/provider integration for user-approved RUSD and CKB-capacity funding.
Funding review showing the exact network, RUSD type script, amount, CKB capacity, and known fees.
Hosted channel onboarding without the user running FNN or manually invoking channel RPCs.
Add-cash and cash-out flows between the hosted channel and the selected FiberNuts mint.
Recovery tests for restart, lost response, duplicate action, wrong network/asset, insufficient capacity, unavailable LSP, and channel-not-ready states.
A security gate covering credential recovery, signer readiness, nonce handling, invoice and preimage authorization, durable storage, and remaining upstream limitations.
Public-LSP interoperability results when the Fiber team’s service is available.
Documented Loop compatibility boundary without implementing or depending on Loop.
Verification:
From a clean client with no local FNN node, connect the supported CKB wallet, review and approve the exact funding requirement, and reach a ready hosted testnet channel.
Add RUSD ecash through that channel and show proofs only after Fiber settlement and mint issuance.
Cash out to a hosted-channel invoice and reconcile principal plus separately displayed mint, LSP, and Fiber fees.

Milestone 3: reusable release, independent pilot, and controlled mainnet validation
ETA: Weeks 9-12
Tranche: $1,500 USD equivalent
Deliverables:

Versioned fibernuts-processor images for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64,withecksums,BOM, dependency report, and release notes.
Operator preflight covering versions, RPC reachability, network, RUSD type script, unit scale, processor registration, TLS, backups, channel capacity, and directional liquidity.
Privacy-preserving health and reconciliation metrics that exclude bearer secrets and user data.
Public design discussion with CDK maintainers and one review-ready upstream contribution through the agreed path. An external merge is not an acceptance condition.
One independently administered FiberNuts deployment built from the public release.
A 14-day public-testnet reliability period with automated smoke checks and reconciliation.
At least 25 hosted-LSP add-cash or cash-out settlements, including nonzero-fee and forced-recovery cases.
One supervised Community Market pilot with at least 10 testers, two vendor roles, and 25 payments finalized by receive-side swap.
Backup-and-restore drill covering the processor journal, mint database, Fiber/LSP state, mint key custody, relay data, client signer recovery, and browser operation recovery.
Controlled direct-channel mainnet validation with at least 10 reconciled operations, subject to the gate below.
Final release, quick start, operations and troubleshooting guides, demo, compatibility matrix, completion report, and six months of best-effort maintenance for critical grant-delivered issues.
Verification:
The independent operator publishes deployment, hosted-channel onboarding, and recovery results from the public instructions.
The testnet report identifies versions, assets, LSPs, operations, fees, failures, restarts, and the resolution of every ambiguous state.
The Community Market report distinguishes token delivery from receive-side settlement and records usability findings without exposing bearer data.
A clean environment installs the package and images, runs the example, preflight, and recovery drill, and links the upstream submission.
Reviewers inspect the final artifacts and either approve the milestone or provide a concrete remediation list.
Controlled mainnet gate
Mainnet validation is limited to the mature direct-channel path. Hosted LSP and Loop are not required, and this is not a public mainnet launch.
Before value is used:
the exact mainnet RUSD script, decimals, and Fiber cell dependencies must be confirmed from an authoritative source;
settlement recovery, backups, preflight, and testnet validation must pass with no unresolved critical or high-severity money-safety issue;
named operators must approve the incident, shutdown, channel-close, and reconciliation plan; and
the run must be restricted to named wallets and a direct channel.
The validation is capped at 50 RUSD total live Cashu liability and 5 RUSD per operation.
Operators supply and retain all RUSD and CKB capacity. Grant funds are not used as reserves or user balances. Published evidence will redact proofs, tokens, quote secrets, user-linked invoices, keys and mnemonics.
If the gate cannot pass, no mainnet value will be put at risk. Any replacement deliverable require a public scope amendment and reviewer approval before the final tranche request.
General milestone acceptance
A milestone is complete only when:
its implementation is merged into the public repository and included in a tagged release;
its verification scenarios run from public instructions in a clean environment;
its report links expected and actual results, known limitations, incidents, and use of funds;
both reviewers have at least seven days to approve or request remediation; and
critical or high-severity money-safety, privacy, key-handling, or recovery findings are fixed before the next tranche request.
External CDK/Fiber merges, the Fiber team’s public LSP launch, and the Loop draft are not payment conditions. FiberNuts-owned code, self-hosted evidence, release artifacts, upstream submissions, and responses to actionable review feedback are the verifiable outputs.
KPIs
Primary KPI
At least 50 fully reconciled public-testnet economic operations: 25 hosted-LSP add-cash or cash-out settlements and 25 Community Market payments finalized by receive-side swap, with zero duplicate Fiber dispatches and zero unresolved mint-liability discrepancies.
Supporting indicators
One project-operated and one independently administered FiberNuts deployment.
One Community Market pilot with at least 10 testers and two vendor roles.
Every tested restart and lost-response case reaches an authoritative terminal or explicitly recoverable state.
At least 10 reconciled operations in the capped direct-channel mainnet validation if its gate passes.
One published cdk-fiber package and one review-ready upstream contribution.
Zero known critical or high-severity vulnerabilities in shipped runtime dependencies at final release.
Public images, checksums, SBOM, compatibility manifest, and operations documentation.
Budget
The total request is $6,000 USD equivalent in CKB.
Work area
Amount
What it covers
Settlement reliability and refund recovery
$1,750
Durable journal, reconciliation, deadlines, events, restart, refund, and fault-injection tests
Hosted-LSP RUSD onboarding
$2,000
LSP adapter, client signing, CKB wallet funding flow, lifecycle recovery, deployment, and interoperability testing
Packaging, diagnostics, and upstream adoption
$1,150
Versioned package and images, preflight, metrics, SBOM, compatibility work, and upstream submission
Pilot, documentation, and controlled validation
$1,100
Testnet services, independent operator support, Community Market pilot, reports, runbooks, and capped mainnet testing
Total
$6,000
The budget does not purchase or subsidize RUSD reserves, user balances, CKB channel capacity, speculative assets, paid votes, or guaranteed routing liquidity. There is no formal third-party audit line, and the result will not be represented as an audited production mint.
Sustainability
FiberNuts remains MIT-licensed open infrastructure:
operators pay for and control their own hosting, reserves, channels, and policies;
mint operators may configure and disclose the standard Cashu input fee;
LSP operators may disclose a service fee, while users pay actual Fiber routing costs when used;
direct bearer handoffs are not charged a central protocol fee; and
reusable packages and upstream-facing work reduce maintenance cost for later operators.
FiberNuts has no token. The developer commits to six months of best-effort maintenance after the final milestone for critical security, money-safety, recovery, and supported-version compatibility issues in the grant-delivered release line.
Key risks and mitigations
Custodial mint: Every balance names its mint, and the UI states that the operator controls issuance and redemption and may impose authentication or KYC.
Hosted-LSP maturity: The adapter is tested against a reproducible operator-run deployment;
external service availability is not a milestone dependency.
Signing material: Root signing material is not sent to the LSP. Recovery, authorization, nonce behavior, storage, and interruption safety are explicit test gates.
User funding burden: The interface states that users supply RUSD and CKB capacity; LSP is not presented as free funding.
Liquidity and solvency: Reachability, capacity, directional liquidity, reserves, and solvency are presented as distinct concepts.
Settlement ambiguity: Missing responses remain pending or recoverable and never authorize a duplicate payment or optimistic balance update.
Bearer secrets: Proofs, tokens, quote secrets, capabilities, signer material, and user-linked invoices are excluded from URLs, analytics, ordinary logs, screenshots, and reports.
Upstream changes: Fiber, CDK, and LSP versions are pinned behind typed adapters and covered by a compatibility matrix.
Mainnet risk: The validation is access-limited, operator-funded, preflight-gated, and capped;
it is not advertised as a public deposit service.
Out of scope
Automatic cross-mint conversion or merging liabilities from separate mints.
Threshold, federated, or script-controlled mint custody.
Trustless exit, proof of reserves, or guaranteed redemption.
Implementing or forking Fiber’s hosted-LSP or Loop protocols inside FiberNuts.
Operating a Loop provider, automated liquidity market, or guaranteed route service.
Public production mainnet mint/LSP operation or unrestricted public deposits.
Formal third-party audit or production endorsement.
Fiat onboarding, free RUSD funding, or grant-funded reserves and channel liquidity.
Lightning/Fiber cross-chain settlement, native mobile wallet, cloud custody, or broad account
system.
Token issuance, central protocol fee, paid marketing, or voting incentives.
Reporting and accountability
Publish a status update at least every two weeks.
Publish one evidence-based report for each payment milestone.
Keep the public project board current with deliverables, blockers, and remediation work.
Record material changes before implementation and obtain community agreement when they affect budget, security boundaries, mainnet exposure, or acceptance criteria.
Give reviewers at least seven days to evaluate each report before requesting the next tranche.
Publish a final comparison of promised versus delivered work and account for the complete budget.
Benefits to CKB
A reusable private-payment adapter for RUSD and other Fiber assets.
A node-light onboarding path that keeps funding and signing responsibilities explicit.
More application-driven Fiber activity through channel onboarding, add cash, cash out, and merchant settlement.
Independently operated mints instead of dependence on one project service.
A standards-oriented bridge to Cashu and CDK without a private mint fork.
Public application, recovery, and operator evidence rather than an infrastructure-only demo.
Closing
FiberNuts has already shown that Cashu bearer ecash can use Fiber as a real RUSD settlement rail The protocol adapter works, public testnet services are available, and the Community Market gives the CKB community a practical way to evaluate the combination.
This proposal focuses the next phase on three barriers to responsible adoption: settlement must recover safely after interruption, users should not need to operate an FNN node, and another operator must be able to reproduce and evaluate the system from public artifacts.
The result remains bounded: FiberNuts will not remove Cashu’s custodial trust model, fund user channels, guarantee liquidity, or claim that availability proves solvency. It will deliver a safer adapter, a public-testnet hosted-LSP path, reusable release artifacts, community validation, and a small gated mainnet proof of the mature direct-channel path.

The following baseline is not funded retroactively:

  • cdk-fiber, implementing CDK’s payment-backend interface over Fiber JSON-RPC.
  • fibernuts-processor, exposing the adapter through CDK’s standard gRPC processor protocol.
  • Compatibility with a stock, unmodified cdk-mintd.
  • Conservative handling of Paid, Received, Pending, Failed, and Unknown Fiber states.
  • Exact network and UDT validation before a Cashu cash-out can probe or pay a Fiber route.
  • A browser wallet with per-mint storage, add cash, send, receive-side swap, NUT-18 requests, cash out, activity, and recoverable operation states.
  • A Community Market attendee application, vendor terminal, capability-scoped payment relay, and bounded public-testnet claim service.
  • Vendor-key-locked NUT-18 payments that the relay cannot redeem.
  • Docker deployment, deterministic Rust and TypeScript tests, browser tests, and opt-in live Fiber tests.
  • Reproducible devnet and public-testnet runbooks.
  • A demonstrated mint-to-transfer-to-cash-out cycle over a live three-node Fiber route with a real routing fee.
  • Public testnet wallet, mint, relay, claim service, and Community Market deployments.

The current implementation is pinned to Fiber v0.9.0-rc7 and CDK v0.17.2. The funded work will validate Fiber v0.9.1 and CDK v0.18.2, or newer stable versions pinned at project start, through code and tests rather than assumptions.

FiberNuts received first place and a final score of 28/30 in the relevant Fiber infrastructure category. That result is evidence of the baseline, not a request for retroactive payment.

Why now

  • FiberNuts has moved beyond an architecture demo: the protocol, public testnet services, bounded claim flow, and attendee-to-vendor application are available for community testing.
  • Public feedback now identifies concrete next barriers rather than hypothetical features: easier onboarding, restart-safe settlement, refunds, clearer risk disclosure, and reproducible operator deployment.
  • Fiber v0.9.1 and CDK v0.18.2 provide stable compatibility targets, while Fiber’s hosted-LSP work is active enough to define and test an operator-run public-testnet integration boundary.

Trust and responsibility boundaries

  • Mint operator: Holds backing RUSD, maintains the spent-proof database, controls issuance and redemption, and may charge a declared Cashu input fee or require authentication.
  • LSP operator: Hosts Fiber connectivity and channel runtime, may charge a declared service fee, and can affect availability and routing. The intended client-signer design does not send the user’s root signing secret to the LSP.
  • User: Supplies RUSD and CKB capacity, approves funding, protects client recovery material, and chooses which mint liability to hold.

Blind signatures reduce direct issuance-to-redemption linkage. They do not hide timing, amounts, network metadata, browser metadata, or operator policy. Browser proofs remain bearer secrets and are not a guaranteed backup.

Team and roles

  • Developer: Code3ks - protocol, Rust, wallet, LSP integration, deployment, testing, and
    documentation

  • Contact: Telegram @code3ks

Relevant track record:

  • Built the reusable cdk-fiber backend and stock-CDK integration.
  • Shipped the wallet, mint deployment, relay, claim service, Community Market, CI, and public testnet services as a solo developer.
  • Demonstrated live multi-hop RUSD settlement with conservative payment-state handling.
  • Received first place and a final score of 28/30 in the prior independent review.

Milestones and staged payments

The project runs for 12 weeks. Funding follows four equal tranches. Every tranche after initial funding follows a public milestone report and reviewer acceptance.

Payment stage ETA Amount Release condition
Initial funding Week 0 $1,500 (25%) Proposal approved and receiving address verified
Milestone 1 End of week 4 $1,500 (25%) Settlement reliability and refund report accepted
Milestone 2 End of week 8 $1,500 (25%) Hosted-LSP public-testnet flow accepted
Milestone 3 End of week 12 $1,500 (25%) Release, pilot, and validation report accepted

Initial funding: baseline and execution setup

  • Tag the grant baseline and publish the milestone board.
  • Pin Fiber, CDK, hosted-LSP, and CKB wallet integration targets.
  • Publish the settlement, signer, browser-key, and refund threat/failure model.
  • Confirm reviewers, independent pilot operator, reporting schedule, and evidence templates.
  • Record the authoritative mainnet RUSD configuration and the validation value cap.

Milestone 1: settlement reliability and refund recovery

ETA: Weeks 1-4
Tranche: $1,500 USD equivalent

Deliverables:

  • Durable incoming and outgoing settlement journal keyed by CDK quote ID and Fiber payment hash.
  • Correct delayed-success accounting for original principal and actual routing fee.
  • Incoming watches and outgoing terminal events restored after processor restart.
  • Deduplicated event delivery with no duplicate Fiber dispatch or balance mutation on retry.
  • Configurable RPC deadlines, bounded retry with backoff, and bounded reconciliation concurrency.
  • Wallet states that distinguish pending, failed, settled, and ambiguous/recoverable outcomes.
  • Clear mint, network, asset, fee, availability, and policy provenance in affected flows.
  • Reviewed NUT-11 refund behavior for expired vendor-locked Community Market payments, including protection against vendor settlement and attendee refund both succeeding.
  • Compatibility matrix and migration notes for the stable Fiber and CDK versions pinned at project
    start.
  • Fault-injection tests for restart, delayed settlement, unknown payment, malformed response, RPC
    timeout, event replay, refund race, fee rounding, wrong network/asset/unit, and secret redaction.

Verification:

  1. Stop the processor during a pending outgoing payment, restart it, and show one Fiber payment with the correct final principal and fee.
  2. Pay an incoming invoice across restart and show one credit event only after Paid.
  3. Make one RPC path unresponsive and show its deadline expire while unrelated reconciliation continues.
  4. Expire and refund a vendor-locked payment, then prove vendor settlement and refund cannot both succeed.
  5. Publish the tagged milestone release, test logs, known limitations, and recovery report.

Milestone 2: hosted-LSP public-testnet onboarding

ETA: Weeks 5-8
Tranche: $1,500 USD equivalent

Deliverables:

  • Typed hosted-LSP adapter isolated from wallet presentation code.
  • Reproducible project-operated public-testnet LSP deployment.
  • Tenant registration, authenticated communication, client signing, and persisted lifecycle state.
  • One documented CKB wallet/provider integration for user-approved RUSD and CKB-capacity funding.
  • Funding review showing the exact network, RUSD type script, amount, CKB capacity, and known fees.
  • Hosted channel onboarding without the user running FNN or manually invoking channel RPCs.
  • Add-cash and cash-out flows between the hosted channel and the selected FiberNuts mint.
  • Recovery tests for restart, lost response, duplicate action, wrong network/asset, insufficient capacity, unavailable LSP, and channel-not-ready states.
  • A security gate covering credential recovery, signer readiness, nonce handling, invoice and preimage authorization, durable storage, and remaining upstream limitations.
  • Public-LSP interoperability results when the Fiber team’s service is available.
  • Documented Loop compatibility boundary without implementing or depending on Loop.

Verification:

  1. From a clean client with no local FNN node, connect the supported CKB wallet, review and approve the exact funding requirement, and reach a ready hosted testnet channel.
  2. Add RUSD ecash through that channel and show proofs only after Fiber settlement and mint issuance.
  3. Cash out to a hosted-channel invoice and reconcile principal plus separately displayed mint, LSP, and Fiber fees.
  4. Interrupt registration, channel opening, add cash, and cash out, then recover withoutduplicate funding, payment, issuance, or balance mutation.
  5. Publish the tagged milestone release, self-hosted LSP instructions, test evidence, and security limitations.

Milestone 3: reusable release, independent pilot, and controlled mainnet validation

ETA: Weeks 9-12
Tranche: $1,500 USD equivalent

Deliverables:

  • Independently consumable, versioned cdk-fiber package with API docs, xampleonfiguration, integration tests, and a supported-version matrix.
  • Versioned fibernuts-processor images for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64,withecksums,BOM, dependency report, and release notes.
  • Operator preflight covering versions, RPC reachability, network, RUSD type script, unit scale, processor registration, TLS, backups, channel capacity, and directional liquidity.
  • Privacy-preserving health and reconciliation metrics that exclude bearer secrets and user data.
  • Public design discussion with CDK maintainers and one review-ready upstream contribution through the agreed path. An external merge is not an acceptance condition.
  • One independently administered FiberNuts deployment built from the public release.
  • A 14-day public-testnet reliability period with automated smoke checks and reconciliation.
  • At least 25 hosted-LSP add-cash or cash-out settlements, including nonzero-fee and forced-recovery cases.
  • One supervised Community Market pilot with at least 10 testers, two vendor roles, and 25 payments finalized by receive-side swap.
  • Backup-and-restore drill covering the processor journal, mint database, Fiber/LSP state, mint key custody, relay data, client signer recovery, and browser operation recovery.
  • Controlled direct-channel mainnet validation with at least 10 reconciled operations, subject to the gate below.
  • Final release, quick start, operations and troubleshooting guides, demo, compatibility matrix, completion report, and six months of best-effort maintenance for critical grant-delivered issues.

Verification:

  1. The independent operator publishes deployment, hosted-channel onboarding, and recovery results from the public instructions.
  2. The testnet report identifies versions, assets, LSPs, operations, fees, failures, restarts, and the resolution of every ambiguous state.
  3. The Community Market report distinguishes token delivery from receive-side settlement and records usability findings without exposing bearer data.
  4. A clean environment installs the package and images, runs the example, preflight, and recovery drill, and links the upstream submission.
  5. Reviewers inspect the final artifacts and either approve the milestone or provide a concrete remediation list.

Controlled mainnet gate

Mainnet validation is limited to the mature direct-channel path. Hosted LSP and Loop are not required, and this is not a public mainnet launch.

Before value is used:

  1. the exact mainnet RUSD script, decimals, and Fiber cell dependencies must be confirmed from an authoritative source;
  2. settlement recovery, backups, preflight, and testnet validation must pass with no unresolved critical or high-severity money-safety issue;
  3. named operators must approve the incident, shutdown, channel-close, and reconciliation plan; and
  4. the run must be restricted to named wallets and a direct channel.

The validation is capped at 50 RUSD total live Cashu liability and 5 RUSD per operation.
Operators supply and retain all RUSD and CKB capacity. Grant funds are not used as reserves or user balances. Published evidence will redact proofs, tokens, quote secrets, user-linked invoices, keys and mnemonics.

If the gate cannot pass, no mainnet value will be put at risk. Any replacement deliverable require a public scope amendment and reviewer approval before the final tranche request.

General milestone acceptance

A milestone is complete only when:

  1. its implementation is merged into the public repository and included in a tagged release;
  2. its verification scenarios run from public instructions in a clean environment;
  3. its report links expected and actual results, known limitations, incidents, and use of funds;
  4. both reviewers have at least seven days to approve or request remediation; and
  5. critical or high-severity money-safety, privacy, key-handling, or recovery findings are fixed before the next tranche request.

External CDK/Fiber merges, the Fiber team’s public LSP launch, and the Loop draft are not payment conditions. FiberNuts-owned code, self-hosted evidence, release artifacts, upstream submissions, and responses to actionable review feedback are the verifiable outputs.

KPIs

Primary KPI

At least 50 fully reconciled public-testnet economic operations: 25 hosted-LSP add-cash or cash-out settlements and 25 Community Market payments finalized by receive-side swap, with zero duplicate Fiber dispatches and zero unresolved mint-liability discrepancies.

Supporting indicators

  • One project-operated and one independently administered FiberNuts deployment.
  • One Community Market pilot with at least 10 testers and two vendor roles.
  • Every tested restart and lost-response case reaches an authoritative terminal or explicitly recoverable state.
  • At least 10 reconciled operations in the capped direct-channel mainnet validation if its gate passes.
  • One published cdk-fiber package and one review-ready upstream contribution.
  • Zero known critical or high-severity vulnerabilities in shipped runtime dependencies at final release.
  • Public images, checksums, SBOM, compatibility manifest, and operations documentation.

Budget

The total request is $6,000 USD equivalent in CKB.

Work area Amount What it covers
Settlement reliability and refund recovery $1,750 Durable journal, reconciliation, deadlines, events, restart, refund, and fault-injection tests
Hosted-LSP RUSD onboarding $2,000 LSP adapter, client signing, CKB wallet funding flow, lifecycle recovery, deployment, and interoperability testing
Packaging, diagnostics, and upstream adoption $1,150 Versioned package and images, preflight, metrics, SBOM, compatibility work, and upstream submission
Pilot, documentation, and controlled validation $1,100 Testnet services, independent operator support, Community Market pilot, reports, runbooks, and capped mainnet testing
Total $6,000

The budget does not purchase or subsidize RUSD reserves, user balances, CKB channel capacity, speculative assets, paid votes, or guaranteed routing liquidity. There is no formal third-party audit line, and the result will not be represented as an audited production mint.

Sustainability

FiberNuts remains MIT-licensed open infrastructure:

  • operators pay for and control their own hosting, reserves, channels, and policies;
  • mint operators may configure and disclose the standard Cashu input fee;
  • LSP operators may disclose a service fee, while users pay actual Fiber routing costs when used;
  • direct bearer handoffs are not charged a central protocol fee; and
  • reusable packages and upstream-facing work reduce maintenance cost for later operators.

FiberNuts has no token. The developer commits to six months of best-effort maintenance after the final milestone for critical security, money-safety, recovery, and supported-version compatibility issues in the grant-delivered release line.

Key risks and mitigations

  • Custodial mint: Every balance names its mint, and the UI states that the operator controls issuance and redemption and may impose authentication or KYC.
  • Hosted-LSP maturity: The adapter is tested against a reproducible operator-run deployment;
    external service availability is not a milestone dependency.
  • Signing material: Root signing material is not sent to the LSP. Recovery, authorization, nonce behavior, storage, and interruption safety are explicit test gates.
  • User funding burden: The interface states that users supply RUSD and CKB capacity; LSP is not presented as free funding.
  • Liquidity and solvency: Reachability, capacity, directional liquidity, reserves, and solvency are presented as distinct concepts.
  • Settlement ambiguity: Missing responses remain pending or recoverable and never authorize a duplicate payment or optimistic balance update.
  • Bearer secrets: Proofs, tokens, quote secrets, capabilities, signer material, and user-linked invoices are excluded from URLs, analytics, ordinary logs, screenshots, and reports.
  • Upstream changes: Fiber, CDK, and LSP versions are pinned behind typed adapters and covered by a compatibility matrix.
  • Mainnet risk: The validation is access-limited, operator-funded, preflight-gated, and capped;
    it is not advertised as a public deposit service.

Out of scope

  • Automatic cross-mint conversion or merging liabilities from separate mints.
  • Threshold, federated, or script-controlled mint custody.
  • Trustless exit, proof of reserves, or guaranteed redemption.
  • Implementing or forking Fiber’s hosted-LSP or Loop protocols inside FiberNuts.
  • Operating a Loop provider, automated liquidity market, or guaranteed route service.
  • Public production mainnet mint/LSP operation or unrestricted public deposits.
  • Formal third-party audit or production endorsement.
  • Fiat onboarding, free RUSD funding, or grant-funded reserves and channel liquidity.
  • Lightning/Fiber cross-chain settlement, native mobile wallet, cloud custody, or broad account
    system.
  • Token issuance, central protocol fee, paid marketing, or voting incentives.

Reporting and accountability

  • Publish a status update at least every two weeks.
  • Publish one evidence-based report for each payment milestone.
  • Keep the public project board current with deliverables, blockers, and remediation work.
  • Record material changes before implementation and obtain community agreement when they affect budget, security boundaries, mainnet exposure, or acceptance criteria.
  • Give reviewers at least seven days to evaluate each report before requesting the next tranche.
  • Publish a final comparison of promised versus delivered work and account for the complete budget.

Benefits to CKB

  • A reusable private-payment adapter for RUSD and other Fiber assets.
  • A node-light onboarding path that keeps funding and signing responsibilities explicit.
  • More application-driven Fiber activity through channel onboarding, add cash, cash out, and merchant settlement.
  • Independently operated mints instead of dependence on one project service.
  • A standards-oriented bridge to Cashu and CDK without a private mint fork.
  • Public application, recovery, and operator evidence rather than an infrastructure-only demo.

Closing

FiberNuts has already shown that Cashu bearer ecash can use Fiber as a real RUSD settlement rail The protocol adapter works, public testnet services are available, and the Community Market gives the CKB community a practical way to evaluate the combination.

This proposal focuses the next phase on three barriers to responsible adoption: settlement must recover safely after interruption, users should not need to operate an FNN node, and another operator must be able to reproduce and evaluate the system from public artifacts.

The result remains bounded: FiberNuts will not remove Cashu’s custodial trust model, fund user channels, guarantee liquidity, or claim that availability proves solvency. It will deliver a safer adapter, a public-testnet hosted-LSP path, reusable release artifacts, community validation, and a small gated mainnet proof of the mature direct-channel path.

recent_posts.topic_title: Ckb-on-ramp：用闪电网络钱包入金 CKB 生态
recent_posts.author: RetricSu
recent_posts.content_text:
最近我做了一个小 demo，叫 ckb-on-ramp，线上测试版在 https://onramp.retric.uk （全部跑在 testnet）。它要回答的问题是：一个手里只有 BTC 闪电钱包、没有 CKB 的新用户，能不能不装任何软件，打开网页就把 BTC 换成 Fiber 通道里的资产？ 我觉得这个想法有意思，是想到如果有这样一个产品，不仅能解决入金问题，也能通过通道网络，让新用户从第一天开始就感受到CKB上二层网络的魅力。onboarding 不一定要 onboard 到 CKB 网络的一层里，二层也许是个更实用的选择。比如入金之后，用户可以直接就去做小额快速的支付，或是直接玩fiber上的游戏。这或许能打开不一样的应用场景。 image2880×1556 241 KB d82c8b602d0f7b745c8c36d18fa7006a2880×1556 210 KB c52a3d4cab2dc13d3b88ed4d9bcd6cb72880×1556 197 KB 7e1015b4b89d4c72c24fc89a6acc16021170×2532 77.7 KB 我自己尝试了下用了zeus 钱包来扫描 demo 里的二维码，换了一点 CKB testnet 上的 cWBTC 的token，体验还是挺有意思的。 这篇帖子简单写下这个 demo 是怎么实现的、我想验证什么、有哪些限制，以及我觉得 Fiber 可以在协议层补上的几项能力。 一、这个 demo 有趣在哪 我觉得有意思的地方有三点。 用户的 Fiber 节点跑在浏览器里。前端用 fiber-js（Fiber 的 WASM 版本），节点密钥由 passkey 保护，状态存在 IndexedDB。用户不需要装 FNN，也不需要懂节点运维。 用户不需要先有 CKB。开 UDT 通道要占用链上 Cell，用户这一侧大约要 184 CKB。对想要入金的新用户来说，这是一个死循环。在这个 demo 里，用了一个比较级简单粗暴的做法：这部分 CKB 由运营方出，可以视为是一种获取用户的补贴。 付款端可以是任何普通的 BTC 闪电钱包。用户拿到的是一张标准 BOLT11 发票，用 Phoenix、Zeus、Blink 之类的钱包扫码付款即可。CCH（cross-chain hub）用同一个 payment hash 把闪电和 Fiber 两边的支付原子地绑定，运营方不托管用户资金。 在 testnet 的端到端测试里，一笔 10,130 sats 的闪电付款，大约 3 秒后测试 Fiber 节点收到了 10,000 raw cWBTC（一个测试网上的udt）。报价规则是 0.3% + 100 sats，差额就是这部分费用。 二、技术原理 整体由三部分组成： 浏览器：fiber-js WASM 节点 + React 前端； 运营方：一个 FNN（v0.9.0），开启 CCH，CCH 连接一个 Bitcoin testnet 的 LND； API：一个 Node 服务，负责报价、开渠协调、替运营方签 funding 交易、调用 CCH 下单。 流程如下： sequenceDiagram participant U as 浏览器 Fiber 节点 (WASM) participant A as On-ramp API participant F as 运营方 FNN + CCH participant L as 运营方 LND participant W as 用户闪电钱包 U->>F: connect_peer（wss） U->>U: open_channel_with_external_funding
（UDT=cWBTC，用户出 0，CKB 来自运营方锁） F->>F: accept_channel，出 1 cWBTC 作为入向流动性 U->>A: POST /api/sign-funding（未签名 funding tx） A->>A: 校验输入/输出/预算后用运营方钥签名 A-->>U: 已签名 tx U->>F: submit_signed_funding_tx → 通道 Ready U->>A: 请求报价，用户生成 cWBTC Fiber 发票 A->>F: CCH receive_btc(Fiber 发票) F->>L: 生成同 payment hash 的 hold invoice A-->>U: 返回 BOLT11 发票 W->>L: 支付闪电发票（HTLC 被 hold） F->>U: 通过 Fiber 通道支付 cWBTC U-->>F: 揭示 preimage F->>L: 用 preimage 结算 hold invoice 下面分几点说实现细节。 外部出资开渠。 最早的版本是运营方先往用户地址转 200 CKB，再由运营方开渠。问题是这些 CKB 成了用户可以随意花的 UTXO，用户领到后可以直接转走。后来我改成用 Fiber 的 open_channel_with_external_funding：用户节点作为 opener 发起，funding_lock_script 指向运营方的锁，funding tx 的 CKB 输入来自运营方的 Cell，找零回运营方；运营方 FNN 作为 acceptor 出 1 cWBTC，作为用户的入向容量。整个过程中用户没有拿到可以直接花的 CKB。 /api/sign-funding 假设客户端可能作恶。 交易由用户的 WASM 节点组装，API 只签满足以下条件的交易：所有输入都属于运营方受信任的锁，输出只有 funding cell 和找零，UDT 守恒，CKB 容量和矿工费都在预算内。 原子性来自 hold invoice。 CCH 的 receive_btc 接收用户的 Fiber 发票，返回一张同 hash 的闪电 hold invoice。用户付款后，LND 端的 HTLC 先被 hold 住，CCH 在 Fiber 这边付给用户；用户收款时揭示 preimage，CCH 再用 preimage 结算闪电那一侧。任一边失败，另一边就不会结算。 收款之后的用途。 前端做了两个出口：用通道里的 cWBTC 支付 Fiber 发票（Spend on Fiber），以及协作关渠，通过 close_script 把 cWBTC 和那部分 CKB 关到用户指定的 CCC 钱包地址（L1 xUDT）。 浏览器节点与运营方的连接。 浏览器里的节点只能通过 WebSocket 连 peer，所以运营方需要对外提供一个 wss 地址。这个 demo 能跑通，前提是运营方节点可以被浏览器直接访问。 三、我想验证的事情 做这个 demo，我主要想验证三件事。 不装软件、不持有 CKB 的首次入金能不能在 Fiber 上跑通。结果是可以，而且整条链路用的都是 Fiber 现有的 RPC（外部出资开渠、CCH、hold invoice），不需要改协议。 浏览器 WASM 节点能不能当作真实的用户节点使用。开渠、收款、付款、协作关渠都在 testnet 上跑过。 这种运营方模式还缺什么。跑下来我的感受是，基本链路已经通了，但让没有 CKB 的用户收款、收回赞助成本、获取流动性这几件事，现在都要应用层自己拼凑。如果 Fiber 在协议层提供对应的能力，做 on-ramp 这类服务会简单很多。下一节主要讲这部分。 四、限制，以及我希望 Fiber 网络往哪改进 先说这个 demo 本身的限制： 每个用户的入向容量固定为 1 cWBTC。不管用户想换多少，运营方都按这个额度开一条渠，每条渠都要锁一份 cWBTC 和约 184 CKB。 赞助的 CKB 可能收不回来。通道 Ready 之后，用户强制关渠就能拿走通道里那部分 CKB。外部出资只是让用户无法在开渠前直接转走 CKB，并没有消除这部分成本。 容量瓶颈主要在闪电那一侧。运营方能收多少 BTC，取决于它的 LND 有多少入向流动性，而 testnet 上这部分很难拿到。 报价不感知流动性。报价接口只检查 Fiber 侧的出资上限，不检查闪电侧还能收多少。额度不够时报价照样能出，但付款会失败。 这些限制大多不是这个 demo 能单独解决的。下面是我觉得 Fiber Ready，用户强制关渠就能把它带走，运营方只能靠限额控制损失。 可以提供什么：开渠时在协议里记录每一方投入的 CKB 容量和对应的退回锁（refund lock）。无论协作关渠还是强制关渠，结算时出资方投入的 CKB 都必须回到它指定的锁，用户只拿走自己的 UDT 余额和自己投入的部分。 大致机制：funding 阶段把容量归属写进双方签署的 commitment / settlement 最近我做了一个小 demo，叫 ckb-on-ramp，线上测试版在 https://onramp.retric.uk （全部跑在 testnet）。它要回答的问题是：一个手里只有 BTC 闪电钱包、没有 CKB 的新用户，能不能不装任何软件，打开网页就把 BTC 换成 Fiber 通道里的资产？

我觉得这个想法有意思，是想到如果有这样一个产品，不仅能解决入金问题，也能通过通道网络，让新用户从第一天开始就感受到CKB上二层网络的魅力。onboarding 不一定要 onboard 到 CKB 网络的一层里，二层也许是个更实用的选择。比如入金之后，用户可以直接就去做小额快速的支付，或是直接玩fiber上的游戏。这或许能打开不一样的应用场景。

我自己尝试了下用了zeus 钱包来扫描 demo 里的二维码，换了一点 CKB testnet 上的 cWBTC 的token，体验还是挺有意思的。

这篇帖子简单写下这个 demo 是怎么实现的、我想验证什么、有哪些限制，以及我觉得 Fiber 可以在协议层补上的几项能力。

一、这个 demo 有趣在哪

我觉得有意思的地方有三点。

  1. 用户的 Fiber 节点跑在浏览器里。前端用 fiber-js（Fiber 的 WASM 版本），节点密钥由 passkey 保护，状态存在 IndexedDB。用户不需要装 FNN，也不需要懂节点运维。
  2. 用户不需要先有 CKB。开 UDT 通道要占用链上 Cell，用户这一侧大约要 184 CKB。对想要入金的新用户来说，这是一个死循环。在这个 demo 里，用了一个比较级简单粗暴的做法：这部分 CKB 由运营方出，可以视为是一种获取用户的补贴。
  3. 付款端可以是任何普通的 BTC 闪电钱包。用户拿到的是一张标准 BOLT11 发票，用 Phoenix、Zeus、Blink 之类的钱包扫码付款即可。CCH（cross-chain hub）用同一个 payment hash 把闪电和 Fiber 两边的支付原子地绑定，运营方不托管用户资金。

在 testnet 的端到端测试里，一笔 10,130 sats 的闪电付款，大约 3 秒后测试 Fiber 节点收到了 10,000 raw cWBTC（一个测试网上的udt）。报价规则是 0.3% + 100 sats，差额就是这部分费用。

二、技术原理

整体由三部分组成：

  • 浏览器：fiber-js WASM 节点 + React 前端；
  • 运营方：一个 FNN（v0.9.0），开启 CCH，CCH 连接一个 Bitcoin testnet 的 LND；
  • API：一个 Node 服务，负责报价、开渠协调、替运营方签 funding 交易、调用 CCH 下单。

流程如下：

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as 浏览器 Fiber 节点 (WASM)
    participant A as On-ramp API
    participant F as 运营方 FNN + CCH
    participant L as 运营方 LND
    participant W as 用户闪电钱包

    U->>F: connect_peer（wss）
    U->>U: open_channel_with_external_funding<br/>（UDT=cWBTC，用户出 0，CKB 来自运营方锁）
    F->>F: accept_channel，出 1 cWBTC 作为入向流动性
    U->>A: POST /api/sign-funding（未签名 funding tx）
    A->>A: 校验输入/输出/预算后用运营方钥签名
    A-->>U: 已签名 tx
    U->>F: submit_signed_funding_tx → 通道 Ready
    U->>A: 请求报价，用户生成 cWBTC Fiber 发票
    A->>F: CCH receive_btc(Fiber 发票)
    F->>L: 生成同 payment hash 的 hold invoice
    A-->>U: 返回 BOLT11 发票
    W->>L: 支付闪电发票（HTLC 被 hold）
    F->>U: 通过 Fiber 通道支付 cWBTC
    U-->>F: 揭示 preimage
    F->>L: 用 preimage 结算 hold invoice

下面分几点说实现细节。

外部出资开渠。 最早的版本是运营方先往用户地址转 200 CKB，再由运营方开渠。问题是这些 CKB 成了用户可以随意花的 UTXO，用户领到后可以直接转走。后来我改成用 Fiber 的 open_channel_with_external_funding：用户节点作为 opener 发起，funding_lock_script 指向运营方的锁，funding tx 的 CKB 输入来自运营方的 Cell，找零回运营方；运营方 FNN 作为 acceptor 出 1 cWBTC，作为用户的入向容量。整个过程中用户没有拿到可以直接花的 CKB。

/api/sign-funding 假设客户端可能作恶。 交易由用户的 WASM 节点组装，API 只签满足以下条件的交易：所有输入都属于运营方受信任的锁，输出只有 funding cell 和找零，UDT 守恒，CKB 容量和矿工费都在预算内。

原子性来自 hold invoice。 CCH 的 receive_btc 接收用户的 Fiber 发票，返回一张同 hash 的闪电 hold invoice。用户付款后，LND 端的 HTLC 先被 hold 住，CCH 在 Fiber 这边付给用户；用户收款时揭示 preimage，CCH 再用 preimage 结算闪电那一侧。任一边失败，另一边就不会结算。

收款之后的用途。 前端做了两个出口：用通道里的 cWBTC 支付 Fiber 发票（Spend on Fiber），以及协作关渠，通过 close_script 把 cWBTC 和那部分 CKB 关到用户指定的 CCC 钱包地址（L1 xUDT）。

浏览器节点与运营方的连接。 浏览器里的节点只能通过 WebSocket 连 peer，所以运营方需要对外提供一个 wss 地址。这个 demo 能跑通，前提是运营方节点可以被浏览器直接访问。

三、我想验证的事情

做这个 demo，我主要想验证三件事。

  1. 不装软件、不持有 CKB 的首次入金能不能在 Fiber 上跑通。结果是可以，而且整条链路用的都是 Fiber 现有的 RPC（外部出资开渠、CCH、hold invoice），不需要改协议。
  2. 浏览器 WASM 节点能不能当作真实的用户节点使用。开渠、收款、付款、协作关渠都在 testnet 上跑过。
  3. 这种运营方模式还缺什么。跑下来我的感受是，基本链路已经通了，但让没有 CKB 的用户收款、收回赞助成本、获取流动性这几件事，现在都要应用层自己拼凑。如果 Fiber 在协议层提供对应的能力，做 on-ramp 这类服务会简单很多。下一节主要讲这部分。

四、限制，以及我希望 Fiber 网络往哪改进

先说这个 demo 本身的限制：

  • 每个用户的入向容量固定为 1 cWBTC。不管用户想换多少，运营方都按这个额度开一条渠，每条渠都要锁一份 cWBTC 和约 184 CKB。

  • 报价不感知流动性。报价接口只检查 Fiber 侧的出资上限，不检查闪电侧还能收多少。额度不够时报价照样能出，但付款会失败。

提案 1：零 CKB 收款，即 Fiber 版的 JIT 通道。

  • 解决什么：运营方垫付的 CKB 是获客成本。现在通道一旦 Ready，用户强制关渠就能把它带走，运营方只能靠限额控制损失。

提案 3：自定义 swap 报价，以及让 CCH 具备流动性感知

最后

从这个 demo 看，在 Fiber 上用浏览器节点加一个闪电钱包完成 BTC 到 CKB 生态资产的首次入金，现有能力已经够用。如果要让这类服务规模化，还需要上面几项协议层面的支持。另一个感受是，闪电网络生态上的钱包，类似 ZEUS 这样的，对普通用户仍然有很大的使用门槛。稳定性和易用性都还有很大的空间。Fiber 如果以后有类似的产品，可以想象也会面临更多的挑战。

recent_posts.content_text:
这个方向挺有意思的。如果这条路径能够跑通，Fiber 就有机会成为用户进入 CKB 生态的第一站，而不必再以 L1 作为必经入口。尤其是通过 fiber-js WASM 在浏览器中运行用户节点，并利用 Passkey 保护密钥，这对网页游戏、即时支付、小额打赏等场景都很有价值。
从长远来看，还可以探索一套可持续的 LSP 商业模式，运营商为新用户开通通道、提供资金和流动性，再通过手续费覆盖成本并获得收益，而不是让冷启动长期依赖无条件补贴。
另外，这对我正在做的 UTXOPlay Store 也有潜在的入口价值。比如未来可以在首页提供一个 Play with Bitcoin 入口：玩家只需要已有的闪电钱包，扫码支付少量 BTC，系统便自动完成 Fiber 通道的建立和游戏资产的获取，随后就能直接开始玩游戏了了
nice work!

Pocket Node v1.8.6
This update focuses on wallet protection and making backup and recovery easier to understand.
Wallet passphrase protection
Set up a separate wallet passphrase that gives you a fallback if Android device authentication becomes unavailable. Optional device authentication remains available for everyday use.
Cleaner settings and backup screens
Wallet protection settings are simpler to navigate, with clearer explanations and a redesigned backup verification flow.
Recovery and reliability improvements
Missing Android security keys now lead to recovery options instead of a crash. We also fixed backup verification, wallet restore, activity export and sync issues, and improved Nervos DAO compensation calculations.

Complete. CKBoost issues ckboost.quest.v1 Claim Cells after confirmed reward or points claims through its own issuer DID and funded server-side signer. A real completion is publicly readable, rendered on the subject’s profile, and scored exactly once.
Vellum webpage improvements covering identity and reputation views, navigation, and copy
Complete. The public landing page now presents the working product and confirmed Testnet evidence, with live paths for builders, issuers, integrators, and community reviewers. Task-oriented documentation covers the same shipped flows.
The GitHub milestone has no open implementation items. It records 10 closed issues and six merged milestone pull requests, together with the linked dashboard follow-up in PR #55 and the upstream CKBoost implementation in Alive24/CKBoost PR #65.
What shipped
Public builder profiles and Claim Cell renderers
Every live Testnet did:ckb can now be opened through a directly linkable public profile. The profile combines the live DID document, optional services.profile data, verified accounts, the current reputation result, accepted and excluded evidence, and the source transaction for each Claim Cell. Direct profile loads work without a connected wallet and expose profile-specific canonical and social metadata.
Known Claim Cell schemas render through an exact-hash registry. Each registered renderer validates its payload before presentation, while malformed or unknown claims remain inspectable through a bounded raw-data view instead of being silently discarded. The shared registry covers every published Vellum schema, including ckboost.quest.v1.
Implementation: PR #52 and PR #53.
CKBoost issuance, rendering, and scoring
CKBoost now reconstructs the campaign, quest, user, approval, and reward provenance after a confirmed reward or points claim. It verifies that the selected active DID controller authorized the reward transaction and matches the approved CKBoost user, then issues through a CKBoost-controlled Testnet issuer. Signed transaction state and issuer coordination are persisted with strong consistency so retries reuse the exact transaction and cannot create a duplicate completion claim.
The canonical ckboost.quest.v1 schema preserves the campaign Type ID, quest ID, CKBoost user Type ID, completion timestamp, raw points, approval transaction, and final reward-claim transaction. The public renderer exposes those fields and transaction links. Raw CKBoost points remain informational; the versioned Vellum policy scores eligible completion depth and campaign breadth independently rather than treating platform points as reputation points.
The active vellum.reputation.v7 policy accepts claims only from the configured CKBoost issuer and a versioned eligible-quest registry. Untrusted issuers, unregistered quests, duplicates, malformed payloads, and ineligible completions do not contribute silently.
Implementation: Vellum PR #56, CKBoost PR #65, and Vellum end-to-end validation PR #59.
Public website and documentation
The illustrative homepage has been replaced by a public product experience centered on portable identity, issuer-backed evidence, and transparent reputation. It exposes the confirmed CKBoost Testnet claim as inspectable product evidence and provides working entry points for identity management, public profiles, schemas, SDK integration, grant progress, and the published reputation policy.
The documentation now has separate task-oriented paths for builders, claim issuers, application integrators, and did:ckb identity resolution. Pages have persistent reference navigation, anchored section navigation, executable SDK examples, and accessible copy success and recovery states. @Ajay for Klaveroq: a trusted work marketplace for talent discovery, milestone delivery, and protected payments.
@Ayoub_Lesfer for CrowdCell: an on-chain crowdfunding platform built on CKB.
Hamza’s Legacy for Kweela: a platform for people, creators, communities, and brands.

recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
Hi everyone,
I’ve been working on UTXOPlay over the weekend, and the alpha is now live at utxoplay.io.
image1920×1111 494 KB
There are currently 13 games listed. It’s still early, and there’s plenty to improve, but I’d love for people to try it and share what works, what breaks, and what feels missing.
image1920×1111 477 KB
image1920×1111 629 KB
image1920×1111 417 KB
image1920×1111 333 KB
image1920×1111 340 KB
I also wanted to put the broader idea in writing: how the platform is structured, how it could bring together technology from across the Nervos community, and how we could work toward community-driven development and DAO governance.
The Nervos community has built a lot of useful technology. UTXOPlay is an attempt to bring some of that work together in something people can play.
Games give us practical problems to solve. A login, a match, a purchase, or an earned item raises questions about identity, execution, verification, payments, and ownership. Players also give us honest feedback. If a game takes too long to load or the controls feel wrong, they leave.
I hope this can become a place where developers try their tools in real applications, learn from players, and contribute integrations that others can reuse.
Community-driven, from the beginning
I’d like participation to extend beyond writing game code. Playtesting, artwork, music, translation, documentation, and maintaining shared infrastructure all matter.
Player feedback should influence development priorities. Creators should be able to bring their own games. People working on ecosystem tools should have a place to test whether those tools are useful and approachable in practice.
That also means giving contributors room to work independently. The platform architecture reflects this:
UTXOPlay handles shared platform services: discovery, accounts and wallet connections, game libraries, creator publishing, and community features.
Each game owns its implementation: rules, rendering, state, runtime, and game-specific services.
The current source separates the store and games into independent repositories. Games can be built and deployed separately and can run without the store. The code is available in the UTXOPlay repository.
A creator should be able to use the platform’s common services while continuing to maintain their own game. Platform development and game development can then move at their own pace.
Myelin first, Fiber next
The first batch of games is Myelin-based.
In UTXOPlay today, Myelin supports off-chain execution, signed records, and replay verification. The aim is to retain a game’s execution history so it can be checked against the exact rules and application profile under which it ran.
There is a boundary worth making explicit: a verified Myelin replay is not a CKB settlement receipt. The current games still have trust assumptions around their hosts and signing authorities. On-chain payments, asset issuance, and transfers require separate integration and verification.
Game updates also need to preserve the meaning of existing records. Old saves and signed sessions should remain bound to their original rules; an update should not silently reinterpret them.
Starting with Myelin lets us work on these foundations through actual games.
We plan to support Fiber-based games as the relevant support and tooling mature. In our earlier community discussion, I mentioned user onboarding, bootstrapping, and LSP support as areas to work through for this direction. Those integration questions will help determine when and how we introduce it.
Fiber opens up possibilities around channel payments and frequent, small transactions. We could explore pay-per-session experiences, payments between players, or games designed around those interactions. The specific design should follow the game and what we can reliably support.
Myelin and Fiber could also be used together: a game might need replayable execution records alongside channel payments. Payment support still leaves game-specific questions about result verification, interrupted sessions, and disputes to resolve.
This is how I’d like to approach ecosystem integration more generally. Wallet connectivity already uses CCC. Where there is a useful collectible, cosmetic, or achievement use case, we could explore Spore and DOB as well. Each integration should make something better for a player or developer.
Two questions from truth that deserve proper answers
In our recent community conversation, truth raised two questions that get to the heart of how a platform like this should work: how publishers and vendors are governed, and whether games can involve staking or winner-takes-all mechanics.
These deserve a place in the design from the start.
Who develops a game, who publishes it, and who is accountable?
truth also asked whether the developer and publisher would always be the same person.
For many small games, they will be. Developers can self-publish. But I’d like UTXOPlay to support third-party publishers too, so the roles should remain distinct.
Teeworlds is a useful example: I’m operating and publishing it on UTXOPlay, while the original game was developed by other people. recent_posts.topic_title: Tactus O1: First Based EVM Rollup on CKB
recent_posts.author: ArthurZhang
recent_posts.content_text:
Tactus 0.02 — making the rollup lifecycle explicit
Tactus 0.01 explored whether an EVM rollup on CKB could work. In 0.02, the focus is making the different parts agree: how transactions enter the system, what order they follow, when their results can be trusted, and what users can do if progress stops.
The most important distinction is between being ordered and being settled. A transaction appearing in the rollup’s history does not, by itself, make its result available for withdrawals.
flowchart LR
A[Request accepted] --> B[Order recorded on CKB]
B --> C[Execution checked]
C -. Next proof milestone .-> D[Proof accepted on CKB]
D --> E[Result settled]
What changes
Deposits and priority requests now follow explicit queues. Once a batch of work is fixed, later arrivals cannot change what it contains. Publishing progress must respect both queues, rather than advancing one while quietly leaving the other behind.
There are limits on how much work can remain unproven. When those limits are reached, new work pauses. The paths needed to make progress or respond to a stall remain available.
flowchart TD
A[Unproven work reaches the limit] --> B[Pause further admission or publication]
B --> C[Settle existing work]
B --> D[If progress stays stalled, use the recovery path]
Reports now distinguish ordered work, settled results, claims that are ready to submit, and payments already included on CKB. Each on-chain observation shows its own confirmation depth. A provisional promise is not shown as settled, and a chain reorganization can change previously reported status.
The system also has an explicit response to a prolonged stall. After the required waiting period, another participant can freeze the instance. Freezing stops new progress and preserves the boundary used to determine each person’s rights.
flowchart TD
A[Progress remains stalled] --> B[Waiting period passes]
B --> C[Any participant can trigger a freeze]
C --> D[Uncredited deposits can be refunded]
C --> E[Supported wallet balances use the settled state]
These rights are different. A deposit that has not been credited can be refunded after a freeze. A normal withdrawal must match its recorded request. An emergency wallet claim needs the owner’s authorization and uses the settled balance. The same entitlement cannot be claimed twice. Fees and payment costs come from external funds, rather than reducing the amount the user is owed.
What we checked
Local CKB networks have exercised full queues, competing submissions, a stalled instance, refunds, node outages and a genuine chain reorganization. Recovery follows the replacement chain and discards rights that existed only on the abandoned branch.
Maximum-size publication transactions were accepted by the local CKB node. The proving program also reproduced the expected results for full backlogs, maximum-size inputs, mixed successful and failed transactions, and heavier computation and signature workloads.
These checks establish execution and protocol behavior. A complete new proof, accepted settlement and the resulting asset release remain the next milestone. We do not yet have an end-to-end proving-speed improvement to announce for 0.02.
What remains ahead
Shared cells still create competition between submissions, and admission fairness remains an open problem. General emergency exits for assets held by contracts are also unfinished; the wallet exit path does not cover every DeFi position.
Next comes the complete proof-to-settlement demonstration. Later work will reduce repeated proving work and measure performance on suitable proving hardware. A separate RISC-V contract experiment will explore execution choices without holding up the main protocol work.
Try it
The release includes the protocol implementation, recovery tools, fixed program files and downloadable test evidence. The getting started guide explains how to check the download and run a local development instance.

recent_posts.topic_title: Twine is up. Try buying and selling CKB without an exchange using Fiber and Nostr
recent_posts.author: ebubedev
recent_posts.content_text:
GTBank is only a payment method on this test desk, for NGN. There is no integration and no relationship with the bank. Zelle is the same kind of label for USD. A coordinator sets the methods on their own desk, for whatever currency they want to support. Twine never talks to the bank. The buyer pays the account the seller types into that trade.
Verifying that payment with the bank is not something this can do. The rules are different in every country, and many banks will not allow that kind of check. The name on the listing is the rail those two people agreed to use. GTBank(for NGN) does not see the trade, does not verify it, and does not guarantee that any CKB moves.
The account name, number, and receipt stay in the trade chat, the same way they do on any other P2P desk. On Twine that message is NIP-44, encrypted to the other person. A relay stores the ciphertext. It can see the two pubkeys and the trade id. It cannot read the account or the picture. The coordinator does not read that chat. A solver can read it only if someone opens a dispute and shares that trade’s key. The solver looks at the history, can talk to both people in that same chat, and then settles it: release the CKB to the buyer, or refund the seller.
Relays keep events they have accepted, and a copy already sent is not recalled. A deletion request does not undo that. The account number is something those relays will store, encrypted, for as long as they store the event.
